description: Believes typeof null returns "null" rather than "object", which is a long-standing quirk of the language.
Believes typeof [] returns "array" when arrays are reported as "object".
Believes NaN is not of type number, when typeof NaN is "number".
Believes typeof on an undeclared identifier throws a ReferenceError, when it safely returns "undefined".
Believes == compares without type conversion, so 1 == "1" is false, or that [] == false is false.
Believes null and undefined are indistinguishable, or that null == undefined is false while null === undefined is true.
Believes NaN === NaN is true, rather than NaN being the only value not equal to itself.
Believes global isNaN and Number.isNaN behave the same; isNaN coerces its argument first, so isNaN("foo") is true.
Believes Object.is and === always agree, missing that they differ for NaN and for +0 versus -0.
Believes decimal floating-point arithmetic is exact, so 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 is true.
Believes Number("") is NaN, when an empty string converts to 0.
Believes parseInt and Number treat trailing junk the same, so Number("10px") is 10 or parseInt("10px") is NaN.
Believes a leading zero makes parseInt("08", 10) parse as octal or give NaN or 0, rather than 8.
Believes empty arrays and empty objects are falsy, when Boolean([]) and Boolean({}) are true.
Believes the non-empty string "false" is falsy, when Boolean("false") is true.
Believes ?? falls back for any falsy value like ||, rather than only for null and undefined.
Believes || and && always return true or false instead of one of their operand values.
Believes optional chaining on null throws a TypeError rather than short-circuiting to undefined.
Believes const makes the referenced object immutable, so changing obj.a on a const object throws.
Believes reassigning a const binding silently fails or succeeds, rather than throwing a TypeError.
Believes let variables read before declaration give undefined like var, rather than a ReferenceError from the temporal dead zone.
Believes var is block scoped like let, rather than function scoped.
Believes function expressions assigned to variables are hoisted and callable before their line like function declarations.
Believes default parameters and destructuring defaults apply for null as well as undefined.
Believes arrow functions have their own arguments object or can be used with new.
Believes map mutates the original array in place instead of returning a new one.
Confuses what array methods return, such as push returning the array or element rather than the new length, or unshift returning the array.
Believes find returns an array of matches or null on failure, rather than the first match or undefined; also that findIndex returns undefined.
Believes slice mutates the original array, or that splice returns a single removed element and leaves the array unchanged.
Believes spreading an array or object makes a deep copy, so nested objects are independent of the original.
Believes sort() without a comparator sorts numbers numerically, when it compares their string forms.
Believes for...in yields array values rather than string keys, or that it excludes inherited enumerable properties.
Believes JSON.stringify keeps undefined and function-valued properties, and doesn't convert undefined array elements to null.
Believes delete on an array element removes it and shifts the others, rather than leaving a hole with the same length.
Believes the in operator checks only own properties, ignoring inherited ones such as toString.
Believes Object.keys lists all properties, including non-enumerable ones and symbol keys.
Believes Math.max accepts an array directly, or that Math.max() with no arguments returns 0 or NaN.
Believes + always does numeric addition, so '5' + 1 is 6, and that - behaves the same way as + with strings.
Believes array includes and Set has have the same lookup cost, or that reduce with spread is as efficient as map.
Believes switch compares cases with == so "1" matches 1, or that cases never fall through without break.
